note: Every bottled Carolina barbecue sauce whose label this project could read on 2026-09-16, plus the bottles it could name but not measure, plus a contrast set of national bottles wearing the word Carolina. Rows are makers in North Carolina and South Carolina except where state is "other", which marks the contrast set. INGREDIENTS are copied in label order, verbatim; upper case where the label or the source database is upper case. A parenthesis holds the sub-ingredients of the item before it. RANKS are 1-based positions among the top-level ingredients: the position of the first item whose own name is a tomato ingredient (tomato, tomato paste, tomato puree, tomato concentrate, ketchup), a vinegar, a mustard, or a sugar (sugar, brown sugar, cane sugar, molasses, corn syrup, high fructose corn syrup, honey, dextrose, apple juice concentrate). An ingredient named only inside another ingredient's parenthesis does not count: the vinegar inside YELLOW MUSTARD (DISTILLED VINEGAR, ...) does not set vinegar_rank. 0 means the label names none. null means no label was found. SUGAR AND SODIUM come from the Nutrition Facts panel of the cited page, divided by the serving's tablespoons. Panels round total sugars to the gram, so a bottle showing 0 g may hold a little, and a bottle showing 1 g in a 2-tablespoon serving is reported here as 0.5 g per tablespoon. A tablespoon of table sugar is about 12.6 g. BASE is this project's reading of the label, applied in this order: mustard, where the label names a mustard and either names no tomato or ranks the mustard ahead of it; vinegar-pepper, where vinegar leads and the label names no tomato; lexington-dip, where vinegar leads and a tomato ingredient follows; light-tomato, where tomato leads but the sugar per tablespoon is under 4 g; heavy-tomato, where tomato or sugar leads and the sugar per tablespoon is 4 g or more; hot-sauce for a table pepper sauce; other where none of those fit. Where no label was found the base is read from the maker's own name or description for the bottle — Golden and Southern Gold as mustard, Vinegar as vinegar-pepper, Red and Sweet Red as heavy tomato — and is other where the maker's wording names a taste rather than a base. Those rows say so in the note. A base on a row with no ingredients is never a reading of an ingredient order. SOURCES: USDA FoodData Central Branded Foods (label data submitted by manufacturers, public domain), Open Food Facts (Open Database License), and makers' own product pages. A sauce whose label could not be found stays in this file with nulls and a note naming what was checked; absence of a row's numbers says the label was not found on this search, not that the bottle has no label.
